items.readable_text:
Content:
If we are given an equation of a plane using the dot product, we can always obtain an equation in terms of [MATH: x,] [MATH: y,] and [MATH: z.] For example, suppose we have the plane that passes through the point [MATH: P(-7,5,-2)] and is perpendicular to the vector [MATH: \mathbf{n}=\langle 3,-6,5 \rangle.]

Content:
First, we note that the position vector of the point [MATH: P] is [MATH: \mathbf{p}=\langle -7,5,-2 \rangle,] and we can write down the equation of the plane using the dot product:

Content:
[MATH: (r − p) ⋅ n|= 0; r ⋅ n|= p ⋅ n; r ⋅ ⟨3, − 6, 5⟩|= ⟨ − 7, 5, − 2⟩ ⋅ ⟨3, − 6, 5⟩; r ⋅ ⟨3, − 6, 5⟩|= − 61]

Content:
Now, to obtain the Cartesian equation, we substitute [MATH: \mathbf{r}=\langle x,y,z \rangle] into the equation above and get

Content:
[MATH: ⟨x, y, z⟩ ⋅ ⟨3, − 6, 5⟩|= − 61; 3x − 6y + 5z|= − 61; 3x − 6y + 5z + 61|= 0.]

Content:
This final equation is called the Cartesian equation of the plane.

[IMG: /graphics/7696c7a1325089f5c28977f94d8be524]

Content:
Note that in the equation
[MATH: {\color{blue}3}x+({\color{blue}-6})y+{\color{blue}5}z+61 = 0,]
the coefficients next to [MATH: x,] [MATH: y,] and [MATH: z] are the coordinates of the normal vector
[MATH: \mathbf{n}=\langle {\color{blue}3},{\color{blue}-6},{\color{blue}5} \rangle].

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we note that the position vector of the point [MATH: P] is [MATH: \mathbf{p}=\langle 9,-2,3 \rangle] and the normal vector of the plane is [MATH: \mathbf{n}=\langle 3,-4,7 \rangle.]

Using the dot product, we can find the equation of the plane as follows:

[MATH: (r − p) ⋅ n|= 0; r ⋅ n|= p ⋅ n; r ⋅ ⟨3, − 4, 7⟩|= ⟨9, − 2, 3⟩ ⋅ ⟨3, − 4, 7⟩; r ⋅ ⟨3, − 4, 7⟩|= 56.]

Now, to obtain the Cartesian equation of the plane, we substitute [MATH: \mathbf{r}=\langle x,y,z \rangle] into the equation above and get

[MATH: ⟨x, y, z⟩ ⋅ ⟨3, − 4, 7⟩|= 56; 3x − 4y + 7z|= 56; 3x − 4y + 7z − 56|= 0.]

Now, to obtain the Cartesian equation of the plane, we substitute [MATH: \mathbf{r}=\langle x,y,z \rangle] into the equation above and get

sections.normalized_html: Find a Cartesian equation of the plane that passes through the point [MATH: P(-3,2,-6)] and is parallel to the vectors [MATH: \mathbf{v_1}=\langle -3, 5, 2 \rangle] and [MATH: \mathbf{v_2}=\langle 1, 3, -2 \rangle.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we note that the position vector of the point [MATH: P] is [MATH: \mathbf{p}=\langle -3,2,-6 \rangle.]

Now, we need to find the normal vector of the plane. To do that, we use the cross product of [MATH: \mathbf{v_1}] and [MATH: \mathbf{v_2}] as follows:

[MATH: n|= v_{1} × v_{2}; = [− 3; 5; 2] × [1; 3; − 2]; = i|j|k; − 3|5|2; 1|3|− 2; = − 16i − 4j − 14k; = ⟨ − 16, − 4, − 14⟩]

Then, using the dot product, we can find the equation of the plane: [MATH: (r − p) ⋅ n|= 0; r ⋅ n|= p ⋅ n; r ⋅ ⟨ − 16, − 4, − 14⟩|= ⟨ − 3, 2, − 6⟩ ⋅ ⟨ − 16, − 4, − 14⟩; r ⋅ ⟨ − 16, − 4, − 14⟩|= 124]

Finally, to obtain the Cartesian equation of the plane, we substitute [MATH: \mathbf{r}=\langle x,y,z \rangle] into the equation above and get

[MATH: ⟨x, y, z⟩ ⋅ ⟨ − 16, − 4, − 14⟩|= 124; − 16x − 4y − 14z|= 124; − 16x − 4y − 14z − 124|= 0; 8x + 2y + 7z + 62|= 0.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
If we are given an equation of a plane using the dot product, we can always obtain an equation in terms of [MATH: x,] [MATH: y,] and [MATH: z.] For example, suppose we have the plane that passes through the point [MATH: P(-7,5,-2)] and is perpendicular to the vector [MATH: \mathbf{n}=\langle 3,-6,5 \rangle.]

Content:
First, we note that the position vector of the point [MATH: P] is [MATH: \mathbf{p}=\langle -7,5,-2 \rangle,] and we can write down the equation of the plane using the dot product:

Content:
[MATH: (r − p) ⋅ n|= 0; r ⋅ n|= p ⋅ n; r ⋅ ⟨3, − 6, 5⟩|= ⟨ − 7, 5, − 2⟩ ⋅ ⟨3, − 6, 5⟩; r ⋅ ⟨3, − 6, 5⟩|= − 61]

Content:
Now, to obtain the Cartesian equation, we substitute [MATH: \mathbf{r}=\langle x,y,z \rangle] into the equation above and get

Content:
[MATH: ⟨x, y, z⟩ ⋅ ⟨3, − 6, 5⟩|= − 61; 3x − 6y + 5z|= − 61; 3x − 6y + 5z + 61|= 0.]

Content:
This final equation is called the Cartesian equation of the plane.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/7696c7a1325089f5c28977f94d8be524]

Content:
Note that in the equation
[MATH: {\color{blue}3}x+({\color{blue}-6})y+{\color{blue}5}z+61 = 0,]
the coefficients next to [MATH: x,] [MATH: y,] and [MATH: z] are the coordinates of the normal vector
[MATH: \mathbf{n}=\langle {\color{blue}3},{\color{blue}-6},{\color{blue}5} \rangle].

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding the Cartesian Equation of the Plane Perpendicular To a Given Vector

Example Prompt:
Find a Cartesian equation of the plane that passes through the point [MATH: P(9,-2,3)] and is perpendicular to the vector [MATH: \mathbf{n}=3\mathbf{i}-4\mathbf{j}+7\mathbf{k}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we note that the position vector of the point [MATH: P] is [MATH: \mathbf{p}=\langle 9,-2,3 \rangle] and the normal vector of the plane is [MATH: \mathbf{n}=\langle 3,-4,7 \rangle.]

Using the dot product, we can find the equation of the plane as follows:

[MATH: (r − p) ⋅ n|= 0; r ⋅ n|= p ⋅ n; r ⋅ ⟨3, − 4, 7⟩|= ⟨9, − 2, 3⟩ ⋅ ⟨3, − 4, 7⟩; r ⋅ ⟨3, − 4, 7⟩|= 56.]

Now, to obtain the Cartesian equation of the plane, we substitute [MATH: \mathbf{r}=\langle x,y,z \rangle] into the equation above and get

[MATH: ⟨x, y, z⟩ ⋅ ⟨3, − 4, 7⟩|= 56; 3x − 4y + 7z|= 56; 3x − 4y + 7z − 56|= 0.]

EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we note that the position vector of [MATH: P] is [MATH: \mathbf{p}=\langle -1,4,8 \rangle.] From the canonical equation, we find that the line is parallel to the vector [MATH: \langle -5,3,2 \rangle.] So, the normal vector of the plane is

[MATH: \mathbf{n}=\langle -5,3,2 \rangle.]

Using the dot product, we can find the equation of the plane as follows:

[MATH: (r − p) ⋅ n|= 0; r ⋅ n|= p ⋅ n; r ⋅ ⟨ − 5, 3, 2⟩|= ⟨ − 1, 4, 8⟩ ⋅ ⟨ − 5, 3, 2⟩; r ⋅ ⟨ − 5, 3, 2⟩|= 33]

Now, to obtain the Cartesian equation of the plane, we substitute [MATH: \mathbf{r}=\langle x,y,z \rangle] into the equation above and get

[MATH: ⟨x, y, z⟩ ⋅ ⟨ − 5, 3, 2⟩|= 33; − 5x + 3y + 2z|= 33; − 5x + 3y + 2z − 33|= 0.]

First, from the coefficients in equation of the plane, we get that the normal vector of [MATH: \Pi] is [MATH: \mathbf{n}=\langle 2,-1,1 \rangle.]

Now, we solve the Cartesian equation of [MATH: \Pi] for [MATH: z\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: 2x − y + z + 13|= 0; z|= − 2x + y − 13]
If we put, say, [MATH: x=0] and [MATH: y=0,] we get [MATH: z=-13.] So, the point [MATH: P(0,0,-13)] lies on [MATH: \Pi.] Note that the position vector of [MATH: P] is [MATH: \mathbf{p}=\langle 0,0,-13 \rangle.]

[MATH: (r − p) ⋅ n|= 0; (r − ⟨0, 0, − 13⟩) ⋅ ⟨2, − 1, 1⟩|= 0.]
